items.question: <ruby>朝<rt>あさ</rt></ruby>、<ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>は<ruby>毎日<rt>まいにち</rt></ruby><ruby>牛乳<rt>ぎゅうにゅう</rt></ruby>を（　）<ruby>習慣<rt>しゅうかん</rt></ruby>があります。
items.reading: Choose the verb that fits the context naturally.
items.explanation: 飲む (nomu, to drink) is the correct collocation with 牛乳 (milk). Milk is a liquid that must be drunk, not eaten or chosen. 食べる (taberu, to eat) is used for solid foods and cannot be paired with liquids in standard Japanese. 作る (tsukuru, to make) is the wrong action—the sentence requires an action of consuming milk, not producing it. 選ぶ (erabu, to choose/select) is incompatible with the meaning of the sentence, which describes a daily consumption habit, not a selection habit.

items.question: <ruby>昨日</ruby>の<ruby>会社</ruby>の<ruby>会議</ruby>で、<u>新しい</u><ruby>企画</ruby>について<ruby>説明</ruby>しました。
items.reading: Choose the correct reading of the underlined kanji.
items.explanation: あたらしい is the correct reading of 新しい, a common N4 adjective meaning 'new'. The い-adjective form is standard here: 新しい企画 (a new project). しんしい (shin-shi-i) is incorrect — 新 can read しん, but the adjective form of this kanji is あたらしい, not しんしい (which is not a real word). あたりしい (atari-shi-i) is a false reading created by confusing 新 with the phonetically similar 当たり (atari, 'hit/approximately'), but the correct reading of 新しい does not contain あたり. あたらい (atara-i) mimics the correct reading but drops the final し, creating a non-existent form; the full adjective stem requires the し sound to be present.

items.question: <ruby>毎日</ruby>、<ruby>朝</ruby>は<u>早起き</u>して<ruby>勉強</ruby>しています。
items.reading: Choose the correct reading of the underlined kanji compound.
items.explanation: はやおき (early rising) is the standard N4 compound reading for 早起き, combining the common adjective 早い (hayai, early) with the noun 起き (oki, rising/waking). That's the correct answer. そうおき is a plausible-sounding mispronunciation of 早 (it mimics the on-reading 早 as そう, but that reading never pairs with 起き in this context—the correct pairing requires the kun-reading はや). はやぎ incorrectly applies ぎ instead of き as the okurigana; while ぎ exists in some verbs (e.g., 起きる is sometimes read as おぎる in very old texts), 早起き has no such variant and はやぎ is not a real word. さきおき confuses the kanji 早 with 先 (saki, before/ahead), a look-alike that does appear in compounds like 先立つ, but 先起き is neither a natural nor a correct reading of 早起き and would change the meaning entirely.

items.question: <ruby>昨日</ruby>は<ruby>駅</ruby>の<ruby>近く</ruby>の<u>薬局</u>で<ruby>薬</ruby>を<ruby>買</ruby>いました。
items.reading: Choose the correct reading of the underlined kanji.
items.explanation: やっきょく is the standard N4 reading for 薬局 (pharmacy/drugstore), combining the common kanji 薬 (やく, medicine) with 局 (きょく, place/shop). くすりきょく (くすり is hiragana for 'medicine', not a kanji reading here) mixes hiragana with the second kanji and is not how this compound is read. やくきょく uses the wrong reading of 薬—the on'yomi is やく, not やつ or やっ in isolation, and moreover 薬局 contracts to やっきょく through a common phonetic rule, not やくきょく. くすりぐみ applies the wrong kanji altogether; 組 (ぐみ, group) does not appear in 薬局, and this word does not exist in the context of a pharmacy.

items.question: <ruby>毎日<rt>まいにち</rt></ruby><ruby>朝<rt>あさ</rt></ruby>、私は<ruby>家<rt>いえ</rt></ruby>を（　）<ruby>駅<rt>えき</rt></ruby>に<ruby>向<rt>む</rt></ruby>かいます。
items.reading: Choose the verb that fits the context.
items.explanation: 出ます (deru/leave) is correct because the sentence describes a daily morning routine: the speaker leaves home and heads toward the station. This is the natural collocation for departing a place. 入ります (ireru/enter) is wrong because it means to go into a place, the opposite direction of the context—you do not enter a house to go to the station. 閉じます (tojiru/close) is wrong because it means to shut something (a door, window, or book), not to depart; the sentence requires a movement verb, not an action on an object. 立ちます (tatsu/stand up) is wrong because it describes standing or getting up from a sitting position, not leaving a location; although it can appear in morning routines, it does not fit the grammatical structure 「家を～駅に向かう」 (leaving home toward the station).

items.question: <ruby>毎日<rt>まいにち</rt></ruby><ruby>朝<rt>あさ</rt></ruby>、私は<ruby>公園<rt>こうえん</rt></ruby>で<ruby>運動<rt>うんどう</rt></ruby>を（　）<ruby>習慣<rt>しゅうかん</rt></ruby>があります。
items.reading: Choose the verb that fits the context naturally.
items.explanation: 「する」is the correct answer because it pairs idiomatically with「運動をする」(do/perform exercise), a standard N4 collocation. The blank requires a bare verb stem to complete 「〜する習慣がある」(have a habit of doing). 「やる」(yaru, to do) is also a common verb, but while 「運動をやる」exists colloquially, it is less formal and natural in the set phrase「習慣がある」context; moreover, as a distractor it tests whether learners confuse similar 'do' verbs. 「行う」(okonau, to conduct/perform) is too formal and literary for everyday speech about exercise habits—it usually modifies abstract nouns like 「会議を行う」(conduct a meeting), not basic activities like exercise. 「練習する」(renshuu suru, to practice/train) is a complete verb phrase on its own and cannot fill the blank without creating redundancy (「運動を練習する習慣」is unnatural); the sentence already specifies the activity as 「運動」, so adding another action verb phrase breaks the structure.

items.question: <ruby>朝<rt>あさ</rt></ruby>、<ruby>家<rt>いえ</rt></ruby>を出る（　）、<ruby>鍵<rt>かぎ</rt></ruby>をかけることを忘れてはいけません。
items.reading: Choose the correct grammar form to complete the sentence.
items.explanation: 前に (mae ni, 'before') correctly expresses the temporal sequence of two actions: you must lock the door before leaving the house. The blank requires a time-relationship phrase connecting 「出る」(leave) to 「かけることを忘れてはいけません」(must not forget to lock), and 前に marks the action that comes first. 後で (ato de, 'after') reverses the logical order—it would mean locking after leaving, which is too late. 時に (toki ni, 'when/at the time of') describes simultaneity or a moment, but does not establish the prerequisite relationship that 前に conveys. 間に (aida ni, 'during/between') refers to a duration or gap between two points, not the logical prerequisite condition this sentence requires.

items.question: <ruby>朝<rt>あさ</rt></ruby>、<ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>は<ruby>毎日<rt>まいにち</rt></ruby><ruby>牛乳<rt>ぎゅうにゅう</rt></ruby>を（　）。
items.reading: Choose the verb that fits the context.
items.explanation: 飲みます (to drink) is correct because 牛乳 (milk) is a beverage that must be consumed by drinking, and the sentence describes a daily morning habit, making the present habitual form grammatically and semantically natural. 食べます (to eat) is wrong because milk is a liquid and requires 飲む rather than 食べる, which is used for solid foods. 読みます (to read) is incorrect—milk cannot be read; this verb pairs with books, articles, or documents, not beverages. 聞きます (to listen) does not fit because it requires an auditory object like music or sounds, not a physical substance like milk.

items.question: <ruby>昨日<rt>きのう</rt></ruby>、<ruby>友達<rt>ともだち</rt></ruby>が<ruby>遊<rt>あそ</rt></ruby>びに来たので、一緒に<ruby>映画<rt>えいが</rt></ruby>を見（　）<ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>い物をしました。
items.reading: Choose the correct grammar form to fill the blank.
items.explanation: The correct answer たり uses the ta-form of 見（みた）plus り to express two or more actions performed alternately or in sequence: "watched a movie and then went shopping." This pattern (verb-た＋り...verb-た＋り) is used when listing multiple actions that make up a single experience, which fits the natural flow of spending time with a friend. たら (if; conditional form) would require 見たら買い物をした, implying "if we watched, then we shopped" — a causal/conditional relationship rather than a sequence of activities. ながら (while; simultaneous actions) means the two actions happen at the same time (watching and shopping simultaneously), which is unnatural here. ば (if; conditional i-form) similarly creates a conditional rather than sequential meaning, not the intended sense of listing connected actions within one outing.

items.question: <ruby>朝<rt>あさ</rt></ruby><ruby>早<rt>はや</rt></ruby>く<ruby>起<rt>お</rt></ruby>きる（　）、<ruby>一日<rt>いちにち</rt></ruby>を<ruby>元気<rt>げんき</rt></ruby>に<ruby>過<rt>す</rt></ruby>ごすことができます。
items.reading: Choose the correct grammar form to complete the sentence.
items.explanation: 「朝早く起きる（ことで）、一日を元気に過ごすことができます」uses the pattern 「V-dictionary form + ことで」to express 'by doing X' or 'through the action of X,' showing a cause-and-result or means-and-outcome relationship. The sentence means 'By waking up early, [you] can spend the day energetically.'—ことで is the correct form here because it marks the means or condition leading to the result. The distractor 「ことが」(koto ga) marks the subject of a clause, but does not express cause or means, so it produces an ungrammatical or nonsensical sentence here. The distractor 「ことに」(koto ni) indicates a target or point of realization ('to the point that' or 'upon'), but does not fit the cause-and-result intent. The distractor 「ことを」(koto wo) marks a direct object, changing the meaning to 'do the action of waking up early as an object,' which does not make sense in context and lacks the causal link needed.

items.question: <ruby>朝<rt>あさ</rt></ruby>、<ruby>会社<rt>かいしゃ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>く<ruby>前<rt>まえ</rt></ruby>に、いつも<ruby>新聞<rt>しんぶん</rt></ruby>を（　）。
items.reading: Choose the verb that fits the context.
items.explanation: 読みます (yomimasu, to read) is correct because newspapers are typically read before going to work — a natural daily habit. 聞きます (kikimasu, to listen/ask) is a real verb but newspapers are not listened to; they are read. 書きます (kakimasu, to write) is grammatically sound but makes no sense — you do not write a newspaper before going to work. 借ります (karimasu, to borrow) means to borrow, but the sentence describes a regular habit of reading your own newspaper, not borrowing one each morning.

items.question: <ruby>毎日<rt>まいにち</rt></ruby><ruby>朝<rt>あさ</rt></ruby><ruby>早<rt>はや</rt></ruby>く<ruby>起<rt>お</rt></ruby>きるのは<ruby>大変<rt>たいへん</rt></ruby>ですが、<ruby>健康<rt>けんこう</rt></ruby>のために（　）ようにしています。
items.reading: Choose the correct verb form to complete the sentence.
items.explanation: 「頑張ろう」(ganbarō) is the volitional form expressing a conscious intention or determination — 'I try to do my best' — which fits perfectly with the speaker's statement about making an effort for health. The sentence structure 「（頑張ろう）ようにしています」(trying to do my best) requires the volitional form in this position. 「頑張った」(past tense: 'did my best') is wrong here because the blank needs a non-past form to attach properly to 「ようにしています」(an ongoing habit/resolution). 「頑張る」(dictionary form) is wrong because it fails to express the sense of volition/intention needed in this context — it would sound more like stating a bare fact rather than a personal resolution. 「頑brevて」(te-form: 'doing my best and...') is wrong because the te-form cannot attach to 「ようにしています」and creates an ungrammatical sentence.

items.question: <ruby>昨日</ruby>の<ruby>会議</ruby>で、<ruby>部長</ruby>は<u>重要</u>な<ruby>案件</ruby>について<ruby>説明</ruby>しました。
items.reading: Choose the correct reading of the underlined kanji.
items.explanation: じゅうよう (重要) means "important" or "critical," and is a common N4 abstract adjective used to describe significance. It fits naturally in the context "explained about an important matter." The distractor おもよう is not a real reading; おも- relates to 重い (heavy/serious), but this particular combination does not exist as a standard word. ちょうよう (長要) is a real but different kanji compound meaning "outline" or "summary," and would change the meaning entirely—the sentence would not fit the context of "explaining." じゅうぎ (重議) is not a standard word and confuses the second kanji; even if it were a word, it would not match the target 要 character.

items.question: <ruby>昨日<rt>きのう</rt></ruby>、<ruby>友達<rt>ともだち</rt></ruby>が<ruby>遊<rt>あそ</rt></ruby>びに<ruby>来<rt>き</rt></ruby>たので、<ruby>一緒<rt>いっしょ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>映画<rt>えいが</rt></ruby>を（　）<ruby>帰<rt>かえ</rt></ruby>った。
items.reading: Choose the correct grammar form to complete the sentence.
items.explanation: 見てから (mite kara) correctly expresses the sequence of events: 'After watching the movie, we went home.' This pattern uses the te-form + kara to show that one action is completed before the next action begins—the natural way to describe a time sequence in past events. 見た後で (mi-ta ato de, 'after having watched') sounds formal/stiff for casual conversation and uses a heavier noun structure inappropriate here; it also requires the ta-form rather than te-form. 見ながら (mi-nagara, 'while watching') indicates simultaneous actions, not sequential ones—we wouldn't have watched and returned home at the same time. 見てしまう (mi-te shimau, 'ended up watching / watched completely') adds a sense of completion or regret, not sequencing, and doesn't fit the straightforward narrative flow of this sentence.

items.question: <ruby>毎日<rt>まいにち</rt></ruby><ruby>朝<rt>あさ</rt></ruby><ruby>走<rt>はしり</rt></ruby>ながら、<ruby>音楽<rt>おんがく</rt></ruby>を<u>（　）</u>いる。
items.reading: Choose the correct verb form to complete the sentence.
items.explanation: The blank requires the i-form (連用形) of 聞く to attach to ～ている (present progressive/continuous state). The correct form is 聞いている, meaning "is listening to music." The sentence describes an action happening at the same time as running: 「～ながら」requires both verbs in their stem/i-form (run-while-listen), and the second verb must then take ～ている to express the ongoing action. 聞く (dictionary form) cannot attach directly to ～ている and would produce ungrammatical 「聞くいる」. 聞いた (past ta-form) is the wrong conjugation here; it would mean "listened" (completed action), not the continuous state being expressed. 聞こう (volitional form) means "let me listen" or "I will listen," which contradicts the simultaneous action pattern and is the wrong conjugation for ～ている attachment.

items.question: <ruby>毎日<rt>まいにち</rt></ruby><ruby>朝<rt>あさ</rt></ruby><ruby>早<rt>はや</rt></ruby>く<ruby>起<rt>お</rt></ruby>きる<u>ことができて</u>、<ruby>健康<rt>けんこう</rt></ruby>です。
items.reading: Choose the correct grammar form to complete the sentence.
items.explanation: The correct answer is 「ことができるので」because the sentence describes a present habitual ability (「毎日朝早く起きる」— waking up early every day) as the reason (ので) for the result 「健康です」(being healthy). The ので construction requires the preceding clause to be in plain present form when expressing a causal relationship with a present-state conclusion. 「ことができたので」(ことができた — could do in past) is wrong because it describes a single past event, not the ongoing daily habit. 「ことができながら」(ながら — meaning "while doing" or "even though") changes the meaning to "while being able to wake up early, I am healthy," which is awkward and unnatural here. 「ことができれば」(conditional form, meaning "if able to") shifts the meaning to "if I could wake up early, I would be healthy," which contradicts the assertion that I do wake up early daily.

items.question: <ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>の<ruby>会議<rt>かいぎ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>間<rt>ま</rt></ruby>に合わせるために、<ruby>今夜<rt>こんや</rt></ruby>は<ruby>資料<rt>しりょう</rt></ruby>を<u>（　）</u>ければならない。
items.reading: Choose the correct verb conjugation to fit the pattern.
items.explanation: The blank requires the i-form (連用形) stem because it is followed by 「ければならない」(must do / have to do). The i-form stem 「準備し」directly attaches to 「ければならない」 to mean 'must prepare the materials.' — The distractor 「準備する」 is the dictionary form (plain present); it cannot attach to 「ければならない」 and would produce the ungrammatical 「準備するければならない」. — The distractor 「準備した」 is the past tense (ta-form); although it is a real conjugation, it does not attach to 「ければならない」 (which requires the i-form stem only) and changes the meaning illogically. — The distractor 「準備できる」 is the potential form; it means 'can prepare' rather than 'must prepare,' and it cannot be inserted into the 「ければならない」 pattern in this position.

items.question: <ruby>毎日<rt>まいにち</rt></ruby><ruby>運動<rt>うんどう</rt></ruby>すること（　）、<ruby>健康<rt>けんこう</rt></ruby>を<ruby>保<rt>たも</rt></ruby>つことができます。
items.reading: Choose the correct grammar form to complete the sentence.
items.explanation: The correct answer で marks the means or method by which a goal is achieved. 「毎日運動すること＋で＋健康を保つ」means "by doing exercise every day, one can maintain health"—で indicates the instrumental means. に (に) means "to/at" and expresses destination or target, not the method used to achieve a result, so it cannot follow 「毎日運動すること」 in this context. を (を) is the direct object particle and cannot mark the instrumental means of an action. から (から) means "from" and marks a source or starting point, not the method or instrument by which something is accomplished.

items.question: <ruby>昨日</ruby>の<ruby>会議</ruby>で、<ruby>部長</ruby>が<u>新しい</u><ruby>企画</ruby>について<ruby>説明</ruby>しました。
items.reading: Choose the correct reading of the underlined kanji.
items.explanation: The correct reading あたらしい is the standard i-adjective form of the kanji 新しい, meaning 'new'. This is the only natural way to describe something as 'new' in everyday Japanese and fits perfectly in this context describing a fresh project proposal. The distractor しんしい (shin-shii) uses the on'yomi reading しん but applies it to an adjective where it does not exist—新しい only uses the on'yomi reading しん as part of the prefix 新 in compounds like 新年 (しんねん), never as the adjective reading itself. The distractor あたらしき (atarashiki) is the classical or archaic kei-form of the adjective, which would never appear in modern business conversation; it would sound stiff and unnatural. The distractor にいしい (nii-shii) attempts to use an alternate or non-standard reading that does not correspond to any recognized reading of 新しい in modern Japanese.
